Accenture Boasts 400 Clients Doing Advanced AI, Notches $18.7 Bn Q4 Revenue

Bookings from Accenture’s eight emerging AI and data partners more than tripled from FY25, while revenue from those partners more than doubled.

Mukundan Sivaraj

Accenture said more than 400 clients initiated their first advanced AI work during FY26, including nearly 100 clients in the June to August quarter, as AI demand continued to expand across its enterprise customer base. Quarterly revenue rose 7% in local currency to $18.7 billion, while bookings reached $22.2 billion.

Accenture’s fiscal year runs from September 1 through August 31.

The consulting and technology services company said clients remain at different stages of AI adoption, with many still building the foundations needed to deploy AI at scale.

“Much of our growth today comes from continuing to build their digital core data foundations and the enterprise AI stack that they need to use AI at scale,” Accenture CEO Julie Sweet said during the earnings call.

The company is also seeing stronger commercial activity from its AI ecosystem.

Revenue from its top 10 ecosystem partners grew 6% in FY26 and accounted for more than 60% of Accenture’s revenue. Bookings from eight emerging AI and data partners more than tripled from FY25, while revenue from those partners more than doubled. 

Accenture has previously disclosed growth in generative AI revenue, though it did not provide a standalone figure in its latest results.

Sweet also acknowledged that AI is making Accenture’s own delivery more efficient.

“We continue to believe the opportunities related to AI are greater than the impact of AI-related efficiencies on our business,” Sweet said.

Accenture highlighted several examples of AI being embedded into business processes. For a pharmaceutical company, it said an AI platform used for clinical-trial planning reduced the time needed to create and analyse trial scenarios from 10 days to 10 minutes, while improving patient-enrolment forecast accuracy by 60%. Accenture said some study designs identified through the platform could shorten trial timelines by up to three months.

The company is also shifting towards more outcome-based work. “Fixed-price work, which includes outcome-based work, is now over 65% of bookings and continues to grow,” Accenture CFO Angie Park said. Managed services bookings reached a record $12.8 billion in Q4, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.4.

Accenture’s shift towards fixed-price and outcome-based work comes as AI enables it to deliver services more efficiently.

The company reported a full-year GAAP operating margin—the percentage of revenue it keeps as operating profit—of 15.4%, an increase of 70 basis points over FY25. It returned $11.5 billion to shareholders in FY26, a 38% YoY increase.

For FY27, Accenture expects revenue growth of 3–6% in local currency and an operating margin of 15.9–16.1%. It expects to invest approximately $5 billion in acquisitions and return at least $9.5 billion to shareholders during the year.

After 18% Rally and 13% Drop, Indian IT Stocks Face AI’s Real Q2 Math

Nifty IT rose 18% and then fell 13% in the July-September quarter. Q2 FY27 earnings will offer an early test of whether AI revenue can offset pricing pressure.

Mukundan Sivaraj
Senior journalist
OCTOBER 1, 2026, 5:46 PM
Listen
5 min
SHARE
Save

Telegram

The past quarter was quite volatile for Indian IT stocks. 

The Nifty IT index climbed 18% from 26,965 on July 2 to 31,823 on August 11. It then fell 13% from that peak and closed at 27,670 on September 29, ending the quarter just 2.6% higher.

Different drivers influenced the rally and the subsequent selloff. 

The July rally came partly as global investors rotated out of crowded artificial intelligence (AI) trades in markets such as South Korea and Taiwan and into India. Foreign investors put more than $1.6 billion into Indian equities that month, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. AIM had earlier reported that the optimism was driven by macro tailwinds from cooling Brent crude oil prices, as well as investors rebalancing their portfolios.

The September selloff brought the AI question back into focus. Investors began weighing whether faster AI adoption would eat into Indian IT’s digital transformation business, even as Indian IT companies reported growing AI businesses.

Market Questions Quality of IT Growth

Indian IT entered the quarter with a growth problem. The AI-driven structural squeeze overshadowed the cyclical lag in client spending.

UnearthInsight Founder and CEO Gaurav Vasu tells AIM that the market has already priced in a weak FY27, with the sector expected to remain in single-digit growth through the year. 

“What makes this more concerning is the quality of that growth,” he says. A large part of the growth has come from acquisitions made over the past two years, and stripping out the M&A contribution leaves organic growth at just 1–2%, he believes.

Global uncertainties, slower client spending, and AI upending the traditional arbitrage model have hollowed out any organic growth. That also clouds investor expectations about the quarter under review. Per Ventura Research, the top five Indian IT companies are expected to deliver subdued growth in Q2 FY27—between 0.5% and 3% on a sequential constant currency basis.

“Q2 financial performance would likely be muted. Discretionary tech spending remains muted,” notes Piyush Pandey, SVP and Lead Analyst for IT, Telecom, Internet, and Power at Centrum India.

Pandey attributes the sharp movements in IT stocks to changing estimates of AI's impact, between deflationary pressure on existing services and the creation of new opportunities.

Sumit Pokharna, Senior Vice President - Fundamental Research at Kotak Securities, believes part of the trend emerges from a shift in client technology spending towards AI. 

“The client’s money has been diverted more to AI-driven [things], and Indian IT services companies were not present in that domain,” he notes.

Vasu says the concern extends beyond Indian IT. He points to declines across global IT services and software companies, arguing that the market is increasingly pricing in the possibility that AI will fundamentally change how enterprises allocate technology budgets.

Both AI Revenue and Productivity are Growing

AI is already showing up on the P&Ls of IT companies.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) reported an annualised AI revenue run rate of $2.6 billion in Q1 FY27, up 13.6% sequentially. It also reported $9.5 billion in total contract value (TCV).

HCLTech's Advanced AI revenue reached $171 million, up 62.1% year-on-year in constant currency. Infosys reported that AI revenue accounted for 8.2% of its Q1 revenue.

The question is whether that revenue is incremental.

TCS's numbers show the tension. Strong deal wins have continued even as AI-led productivity puts pressure on the economics of traditional services. AI can also reduce the teams and effort required to deliver work within existing engagements.

Wipro Chief Technology Officer Sandhya Arun said the company's AI initiatives had created capacity equivalent to 20,000 employees, with that capacity redeployed elsewhere in the business.

That is a productivity gain. It becomes a revenue-growth story only if the company can turn the freed capacity into additional work.

AI activity and AI revenue do not necessarily mean incremental revenue. A company can report a growing AI business while also losing revenue from traditional services that AI has made cheaper to deliver.

Pokharna says AI deflation is already becoming visible in the base business and expects pricing pressure to continue.

AI May Widen the Gap

The pressure will vary across Indian IT companies.

Pandey says tier-2 IT companies are better placed to navigate the shift. Vasu expects investors to move towards moderately growing mid-tier companies if larger firms continue to disappoint.

“Challengers continue to offset this with their sheer gains or strong execution, while the incumbents are largely defending the existing revenues,” Pokharna notes.

Persistent Systems, Coforge, and Mphasis have been growing faster than several of their larger peers, while some have also reported strong AI-related deal activity. They are winning engineering, modernisation, and transformation projects can create new sources of revenue as AI changes the way existing services are delivered.

Persistent, for example, has highlighted AI execution, deal wins, and productivity. Its revenue per employee had risen 58.2% between FY22 and Q2 FY26. 

Coforge provides a recent example. In Q1 FY27, the company said 86% of its revenue came from AI-led engineering, data, and cloud services, while 30% of its active delivery projects were already using its AI assets.

But faster growth does not show whether those AI-led deals are replacing revenue lost elsewhere. Organic growth, revenue per employee, and the ability to turn AI productivity into higher-value work will matter more than the number of AI projects announced.

Q2 Earnings Will Offer a Reality Check

Expectations are already low.

“The main reason is AI deflation and, to a lesser extent, weaker macros [which] will continue to weaken the growth,” Pokharna says. He expects muted growth despite the seasonally strong quarter.

Vasu sees Accenture's results as another signal for Indian IT. If the global IT services company's numbers disappoint, he expects further pressure on the sector and a possible rotation away from slower-growing large firms towards mid-tier companies.

Pokharna says the market's concern has shifted.

“In between, the big question which came to the minds of the investors [was], will these Indian IT companies exist or not going forward? So, we believe that concern is behind us,” he says.

Revenue growth will matter, but the organic component will matter more than headline growth. Investors will also be watching whether large AI-led TCV converts into production work and billing, and whether pricing and margins hold as productivity improves. Headcount, utilisation and revenue per employee will show whether companies are becoming more efficient while continuing to grow.

Q2 will not settle the debate over AI's economics in Indian IT. It should, however, give investors a clearer indication of whether AI activity is translating into revenue.

The US can restrict where an NVIDIA chip is shipped without necessarily preventing a Chinese company from remotely accessing that chip's computing power once it is installed in another country.

Oracle and Chinese tech giant Tencent have agreed to a five-year lease worth $7 billion across the former’s data centres in south-east Asia, the Financial Times reported. 

This marks Tencent’s largest overseas lease deal, and Oracle is providing access to 1,00,000 ‘advanced AI chips’ that are otherwise not available in China. 

This development comes as the US tightens restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, particularly NVIDIA’s high-end accelerators. 

The country has restricted the export, reexport and in-country transfer of advanced computing chips and systems to China and certain Chinese-headquartered entities.

Yet, the Tencent deal illustrates a significant complication in those controls: the US can restrict where an NVIDIA chip is shipped without necessarily preventing a Chinese company from remotely accessing that chip’s computing power once it is installed in another country.

Under the current export-control framework, a Chinese company cannot simply have a restricted NVIDIA accelerator shipped to a data centre in China.

But if the accelerator is legitimately installed in a data centre in a country where its export is permitted, a company can potentially rent that data centre's computing capacity and send workloads to the GPU remotely.

A recent Reuters legal analysis describes almost exactly this scenario: a Chinese company could potentially become an infrastructure-as-a-service customer at a Malaysian data centre and remotely use advanced computing hardware it could not receive in China. 

The report notes that US rules currently do not comprehensively prohibit this kind of ordinary remote access.

Tencent is not alone. ByteDance and Alibaba are already among the largest Chinese users of south-east Asian data-centre capacity. 

Chinese companies have increasingly reserved large amounts of capacity in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and other regional markets as domestic access to advanced GPUs has become more constrained. 

Tencent develops the Hunyuan family of AI models and has been expanding into agentic AI, with products such as WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy and Yuanbao designed to execute multi-step tasks rather than simply generate responses. 

Its latest Hy3 and Hy4 models have been trained and optimised specifically for reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads.

Google DeepMind Builds Watermarking System to Identify AI-Generated Protein Designs

Google DeepMind's approach attempts embeds provenance information at the point where the AI model generates the biological design.

Shalini Mondal
OCTOBER 1, 2026, 2:01 PM
Listen
5 min
SHARE
Save
FOLLOW
Preferred Source
Google News
WhatsApp
Telegram

Google DeepMind has developed SynthID Bio, an AI watermarking system designed to identify proteins and biological structures generated by AI models, as researchers and biosecurity experts grapple with a new challenge—determining whether a biological design came from an AI system, even when it does not resemble any known natural or hazardous sequence.

The system embeds a detectable signature into AI-generated protein sequences and predicted 3D structures without significantly changing their biological properties, according to Google DeepMind. In laboratory testing, the company said watermarked protein designs retained their ability to function and bind to their intended targets.

The development is significant because AI models are increasingly being used to design proteins and other biological molecules. Protein design models can generate sequences that do not exist in nature. That creates a gap for existing screening systems, which largely depend on recognising known biological patterns or similarities.

Conventional DNA synthesis screening can compare submitted sequences against databases of known pathogens or hazardous organisms, but an AI-designed sequence could be novel and therefore have no obvious match.

SynthID Bio intends to add another layer. Rather than only asking about a biological sequence, screening systems could also ask whether it was generated by an AI model.

Google DeepMind embeds provenance information at the point where the AI model generates the biological design.

For 3D protein structures, Google DeepMind modifies atomic coordinates in predicted structures to embed a watermark. The company has also fine-tuned part of the AlphaFold 3 diffusion network so that the predicted structures contain a detectable signature.

This makes the technology different from simply attaching metadata to an AI-generated file. The provenance signal is embedded in the biological design itself.

That matters because metadata can be stripped when a design moves between software systems, while a biological watermark is intended to remain associated with the sequence or structure.

The potential application extends beyond identifying AI-generated proteins.

DNA synthesis providers already screen sequences for synthesis against biological risks. But increasingly capable AI models can generate novel biological sequences that may not closely resemble known hazardous sequences.

A watermark could give synthesis providers another signal during screening about whether a sequence originated from a model that uses the watermarking technology. The system could therefore create a link between AI model developers, biological design outputs, and downstream synthesis providers.

For companies developing AI biology models, this could also create a mechanism to demonstrate that their systems have safety measures built into the generation process.

However, the company acknowledges that watermarking is not a complete biosecurity solution. A major open question is how resistant such watermarks are to deliberate modification or attempts to remove them from AI-generated biological designs.

IBM Partners With IIT Bombay, IISc on Agentic AI, Sovereign AI, Quantum Computing

The research will cover Indic language models, multimodal systems, enterprise knowledge retrieval, and quantum-HPC workflows.

IBM has expanded its research collaborations with IIT Bombay and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) to work on agentic AI, sovereign AI, quantum computing, and next-generation computing systems.

The collaboration will cover sovereign and Indic language model adaptation, multimodal AI, AI infrastructure, and knowledge retrieval. IBM and IIT Bombay have been working together since 2018.

The organisations will explore techniques to adapt and optimise sovereign and Indic language models for Indian languages. The research will also cover multimodal AI systems for software programming education, human-AI collaboration and operations across hybrid cloud environments.

The partners will also work on knowledge retrieval systems that can provide faster access to enterprise information. The research will include AI runtime optimisation and distributed inference to improve the performance and scalability of large language models.

With IISc, IBM will continue research in agentic systems, AI applications, and quantum computing. The collaboration began in 2021.

What's your take on this story?

ADD YOUR COMMENT

“Our collaborations with IIT Bombay and IISc bring together world-class academic research and IBM's scientific expertise to solve some of the most complex challenges in these areas,” Amith Singhee, Director, IBM Research India and CTO, IBM India and South Asia, said in a statement.

Prof Ganesh Ramakrishnan, Institute Chair Professor at IIT Bombay’s Department of Computer Science and Engineering, said the collaboration will cover multimodal AI models, knowledge retrieval, optimisation techniques, agentic AI workflows, and AI-assisted software engineering and education.

“By bringing together complementary strengths in AI, language, knowledge and intelligent computing, we envision trustworthy, inclusive, and scalable AI technologies that can transform how people learn, work, and access knowledge in India and across the world,” Prof Ramakrishnan said.

The IBM-IISc collaboration will involve lightweight time-series foundation models based on IBM’s Granite model family for energy analytics. The models will be used for forecasting, anomaly detection, load disaggregation, and energy optimisation. The partners will also contribute benchmark datasets to support further research.

In quantum computing, IBM and IISc will explore orchestration between quantum and high-performance computing systems. The research will include quantum-HPC algorithms and quantum subspace iteration methods using approximation-tolerant classical diagonalisation algorithms.

“IISc and IBM bring complementary research strengths to jointly explore intelligent, cloud-native platforms that can reason, adapt and orchestrate quantum-classical, edge AI and agentic workflows at scale,” Yogesh Simmhan, Professor in the Department of Computational and Data Sciences at IISc, said.

The company said its agents now handle more than 15 million conversations each week, up threefold since February.

ElevenLabs has raised its valuation to $22 billion after closing a $300 million employee tender offer, doubling its valuation from the Series D round in February this year.

The tender offer was led by Wellington Management and T Rowe Price, with EQT, Goldman Sachs, GIC, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Sapphire Ventures, and BDT & MSD Partners investing in the company for the first time. Existing investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Lightspeed Venture Partners and ICONIQ Capital also participated.

Enterprise customers now account for 55% of ElevenLabs’ revenue, with businesses using its ElevenAgents platform to deploy AI agents for customer support and business operations.

“AI should interact with people the way we interact with each other,” said Mati Staniszewski, Co-Founder and CEO of ElevenLabs. “Getting this right will help ensure AI diffuses widely across the economy, and everyone is able to shape and benefit from it, regardless of technical skill.”

ElevenLabs, founded in 2022, has grown to more than 800 employees. The company said the latest tender offer is part of its effort to give employees regular opportunities to sell shares and participate in the value created by the business.

ElevenAgents now handles more than 15 million conversations each week, three times the volume recorded in February. The company said the platform’s annual recurring revenue has also increased more than threefold over the same period.

The agents are being used for tasks including processing refunds and exchanges, renewing insurance policies, upgrading phone plans, booking healthcare appointments and accessing public services.

What's your take on this story?

ADD YOUR COMMENT

ElevenLabs said its technology is now used in the daily operations of five of the world’s 10 largest technology companies, five of the 10 largest insurers and four of the 10 largest telecom companies.

Customers using ElevenAgents include Stripe, Deutsche Telekom, DoorDash’s SevenRooms, Admiral, Customers Bank and Cadence. Governments in Ukraine and Greece are also using the platform.

The company said voice agents resolve customer issues 31% faster than chat agents on average, based on an analysis of its customers.

ElevenLabs is also seeing more companies use its platform across multiple channels. The number of companies deploying multichannel support with ElevenAgents has doubled since February, with businesses connecting interactions across channels such as WhatsApp, phone calls and email.

The company has built vertical-specific solutions for financial services, healthcare, government, retail and telecoms, with industry-specific integrations and model configurations.

Alongside its agent platform, ElevenLabs continues to develop speech and audio models. The company recently released Eleven v4 and v4 Turbo, which it described as its fastest text-to-speech models.

ElevenLabs said its models can speak, listen and translate in more than 90 languages spoken natively by more than 5.5 billion people. It also recently released Scribe v2 Medical, a transcription model focused on healthcare.

The company said it follows a full-stack approach covering research, product development and deployment. Its engineers work with customers to configure models and agents for specific industries, languages and use cases.

Google has announced its new frontier AI model, the Gemini 4 Argon. The model is rolling out to a set of the company’s trusted cybersecurity partners. 

According to benchmark results, the model outperforms OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 on several coding, science, computer use and knowledge work evaluations. 

The company shared the model’s performance on numerous internal tasks. The model helped save over 300 TiB of memory in the company’s data centres by applying various optimisations. 

In addition, Argon’s agents are helping the company migrate C/C++ codebases to Rust. 

In one completed libgav1 optimisation, Argon started with an existing Rust port of Google’s open-source video decoder and replaced 32,000 lines of SIMD code.

Google plans to expand access to paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers before a broader rollout. Introductory pricing is set at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Gemini 4 Argon ends a long wait for Google, after OpenAI and Anthropic pulled ahead in the frontier AI model race in recent months.

However, reports already show the model struggling. Bloomberg reported on the day of the launch that some Google employees with direct access to Gemini 4 believe its benchmark performance does not fully translate to real-world use. 

Sources told the media outlet that the model struggles with certain coding tasks when employees use it, despite performing strongly on industry benchmarks.

Enterprise-focused Yellow.ai has launched Nexus EDGE, an agentic AI desktop application to automate employee IT, human resources (HR), and operations support. 

The application is designed to identify and resolve workplace issues directly on employees' computers using company knowledge and enterprise systems.

"For a decade, employee help tools have competed on how fast they can answer a question," Raghu Ravintula, Co-founder and CEO of Yellow.ai, said in a statement. "But employees were never asking for answers. They were asking to get on with their day."

Nexus EDGE extends Yellow.ai’s Nexus Universal Agentic Interface to employees' desktops. It is designed to address common problems, such as VPN failures, software installation issues, and difficulties accessing enterprise applications.

Nexus EDGE combines a cloud-based reasoning system, called Nexus Agent, with a local agent installed on employees' computers. The cloud agent uses company knowledge bases, standard operating procedures, and backend enterprise applications to identify solutions. The desktop agent examines the screen and application state and executes the required fixes locally, according to Yellow.ai.

Nexus EDGE supports 114 enterprise tools across 18 categories from deployment, according to the company's product documentation. These include IT service management, identity management, and workplace applications such as ServiceNow, Jira, Okta, Slack, and Microsoft 365.

The system requires employees to approve actions before execution. Yellow.ai said the application operates within the signed-in user's existing permissions and maintains an audit trail of actions across IT, HR, and operations. The company also describes its architecture as designed to keep sensitive data on the employee's device.

The company expects the application to reduce support tickets and return multiple hours per employee annually to productive work. However, it has not disclosed independently verified performance results or quantified reductions in support tickets.

"Nexus changed how enterprises handle customer conversations. Nexus EDGE does the same thing for the people inside the enterprise," said Rashid Khan, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of Yellow.ai.

Yellow.ai said its enterprise AI platform serves more than 650 customers across the US, the Middle East, India, Asia-Pacific, and South America. The launch expands its agentic AI offerings into desktop-based employee experience automation.

The initiative brings BHASHINI's multilingual Language AI capabilities into the CAG’s institutional translation workflows, with a focus on contextual translation, consistent terminology and output quality.

The platform has also been designed around institutional requirements including controlled access, security and data sovereignty, while keeping human oversight within the translation process.

CAG-BHASHINI Anuvaad is intended to support the translation of official and audit-related documents rather than operate as a standalone consumer translation tool. The system is being customised to meet the CAG's language and terminology requirements.

The move builds on an earlier collaboration between the CAG and the Digital India BHASHINI Division. In November 2025, the two organisations signed an MoU to deploy BHASHINI across more than 200 CAG offices for multilingual and multimodal communication, including translating reports, surveys, and evidence, as well as vetting translated and transcribed communications.

The latest launch takes that collaboration further by introducing a dedicated translation environment for CAG documents.

The initiative aims to make audit findings and official information available to a wider audience across Indian languages.

CAG officials said using language AI could reduce linguistic barriers while retaining institutional review and oversight.

By integrating language technology into our institutional processes, we can make communication more accessible, timely and effective, while strengthening the use of Indian languages in governance and official work,” Nilotpal Goswami, Additional Deputy Comptroller and Auditor General (Rajbhasha), said. “The CAG-BHASHINI initiative is an important step in bringing this convergence of language and technology into practice.” 

CAG chief K Sanjay Murthy also highlighted the need to make audit findings and reports accessible to citizens in languages they understand, while supporting the wider use of Hindi and other Indian languages in official work.

Amitabh Nag, CEO of the Digital India BHASHINI Division, highlighted the expansion of BHASHINI from language data and AI models into applications and public-sector use cases.

According to the division, BHASHINI currently supports 36 Indian text languages, 23 Indian voice languages and 35 international languages. Its applications include multilingual agricultural advisory services, voice-enabled grievance registration and conversational services delivered through voice and telephone interfaces.

The CAG deployment adds another institutional use case: integrating multilingual AI directly into preparing and disseminating official documents.

The CAG-BHASHINI collaboration also extended to Hindi Pakhwada 2026, held from September 14 to 29.

Alongside conventional activities such as Hindi noting and drafting, translation and typing competitions, CAG employees participated in language activities and games developed using BHASHINI technology.

The broader collaboration demonstrates how government institutions are beginning to use language AI not only for translation but also for internal language engagement and official workflows.

The CAG-BHASHINI Anuvaad launch therefore marks a shift from using AI as an experimental language tool to embedding multilingual AI within an institutional process where translation accuracy, terminology, security, data control and human review are critical.

SmartBear released findings from its 2026 State of Software Quality and Testing report. The company said 46% of surveyed teams have shipped AI-generated code that later failed in production.

The survey covered 1,436 technology professionals whose organisations use AI in development, according to the company. Respondents are based in the United States, the United Kingdom, or other countries, as per the report.

Among teams that had shipped failed code, 69% still have a lot or complete confidence that AI-written code behaves as intended, the company said. Across all respondents, 73% of leaders hold that level of confidence, compared with 52% of practitioners, according to SmartBear.

“AI coding failures are already costing companies revenue, customers, and trust, yet leaders remain blindly confident that AI-generated code behaves as intended, even after watching it fail,” said Dan Faulkner, Chief Executive Officer of SmartBear. “Closing the gap between perception and reality demands quality and testing built for AI’s speed, complexity, and scale.”

According to the company, 95% of leaders and 86% of practitioners are confident their AI agents’ work is adequately reviewed. The company said only 25% of teams have humans reviewing more than 80% of what those agents produce.

SmartBear said teams that review more agent output reported fewer failures, though failures remained common in both groups. As per the report, 49% of teams reviewing more than 60% of agent output have shipped AI code that later failed, compared with 58% of teams reviewing 60% or less.

The company said 47% of organisations cannot explain how AI contributed to a bug or incident in production. According to the report, that figure rises to 73% among teams that have already shipped a failure.

SmartBear said 46% of teams check that the specification reflects intent before AI generates code from it. The report describes that point as the earliest and least costly place to catch a problem.

The company said 69% of US respondents now say AI writes or accelerates at least 41% of their code, compared with 43% in its January 2026 Closing the AI Software Quality Gap report. SmartBear also reported that 45% of US respondents are very or extremely concerned about application quality, up from 36% in January.

The company said 83% of respondents believe autonomous testing, in which AI agents generate, execute, adapt, and report on tests without manual scripting, would help them keep pace with AI code volume. According to SmartBear, 23% named trust in the results as the top barrier to adopting it, compared with 12% who named cost.

The company said 84% of respondents use at least one form of human review to validate AI-generated tests, while 3% rely on AI self-validation alone.

SmartBear said AI-powered testing and validation tools can help companies achieve application integrity, which it defines as continuous, measurable assurance that software works as intended.

Tech Mahindra has partnered with industrial technology company Infinite Uptime to accelerate physical AI adoption across manufacturing and process industries.

The partnership will combine Infinite Uptime’s PlantOS, an industrial outcome intelligence engine, with Tech Mahindra’s manufacturing expertise, global reach, and IT-OT transformation capabilities.

The companies said the partnership will help manufacturers move from predictive insights to prescribed actions by embedding industrial intelligence into plant workflows and tracking its impact on production performance.

Infinite Uptime’s PlantOS combines mechanical and process signals with physics-aware contextualisation and failure-mode intelligence. It provides recommendations on what action to take, why it is required, and when it should be completed, according to the company.

The approach is similar to recent industrial AI efforts that use models to determine interventions rather than simply predict outcomes. For example, factory optimisation using physical AI has focused on using AI to determine interventions that can affect real-world production outcomes.

The partnership will target steel, cement, chemicals, metals and mining, pulp and paper, and other asset-intensive industries, where industrial AI is also being applied to areas such as predictive maintenance and operational intelligence. The initial focus will be North America and Europe, particularly larger transformation programmes where equipment reliability and production performance are closely linked.
